title: Two bowls, swapped
hookLine: two bowls swapped in a kitchen, and a family of sages raises a fighter
carry: svadharma: your dharma follows your nature
tomorrow: his father gives an order no son should get. what does he do?
last: THE THIRD STRIDE MEASURES A PERSON.

lines: A SAGE'S SON WITH AN AXE.
cards: Somebody grabs the wrong coffee cup. Here's an older version. Parashurama is a sage's son who carries a warrior's axe, and in the world of these stories that's strange: priests study, warriors fight.
The Bhagavata explains it with a mix-up in a kitchen. Two bowls of blessed rice pudding, one for a priest's calm, one for a warrior's fire. And the two women they were meant for swap them.

teach.b: The sage Richika blesses two portions: one for his wife, Satyavati, to bear a son with a priest's calm; one for her mother, to bear a son with a warrior's fire.
Her mother guesses a husband would bless his own wife's bowl best, and talks her daughter into a swap. When Richika finds out, he tells Satyavati what it means: her son will be fierce.

She pleads, and he grants this much: the fire will skip a generation. So her son, Jamadagni, grows up a calm and learned sage. And Jamadagni's son, with his wife Renuka, is the one who carries the fire.
That's Parashurama. His name puts parashu, an axe, beside the name Rama; tradition says Shiva gave him the axe. And the other bowl?

teach.h: VISHVAMITRA: THE KING WHO BECAME A SAGE.
teach.b: Many tellings say it went the other way: Satyavati's brother, Vishvamitra, was born a king and became one of the greatest sages. So what were the bowls carrying? A nature.
Old Hindu thought names four callings, the varnas: priests and teachers, rulers and warriors, traders, and workers.

teach.h: GUNA AND KARMA: NATURE AND WORK.
teach.b: In the Gita, Krishna says those callings follow guna and karma, a person's qualities and their work, and that it's better to live your own dharma, svadharma, imperfectly than someone else's well.
For centuries, varna was mostly fixed by birth and hardened into caste, which many Hindu teachers have challenged.
Many readers hear this story as a door left open: a sage's son with a warrior's fire, a king's son who becomes a sage. And today?
When a family says 'we're all doctors' and a kid has a firefighter's fire, the Gita's question isn't 'what's your family name?' It's 'what's your nature, and what work will you do with it?'

how: Parashurama is honored as a form of Vishnu, and some Hindus keep a day for him, Parashurama Jayanti, around the spring festival of Akshaya Tritiya.

o: a warrior king who stole a sage's cow
Rama with the axe, a sage's son with a warrior's fire
Rama's younger brother, who fought at Lanka

games.q: who's who in the kitchen — tap the pairs.
p: pleads: let the fire skip a generation
born a king, became a sage

s: Parashurama is the same Rama as in the Ramayana
he's another form of Vishnu: Rama with the axe, a sage's son.
Jamadagni is the fierce one in the family
the fire skips him; he grows up calm and learned.
in the Gita, Krishna ties the four callings to a person's qualities and work
guna and karma: nature and work, not a family name alone.

games.q: your cousin's whole family are doctors, and she wants to be a firefighter. her grandpa says 'that's not who we are.' what would Parashurama's story notice?
o: her svadharma has to fit her nature; the Gita ties callings to qualities and work.
grandpa's right; the bowls prove nature comes down through the family line.
the story has nothing at all to say about callings.
games.why: the fire came with a blessing, not a family name, and Krishna ties the callings to guna and karma: who you are and what you do.

practice: Sit tall, as steady as someone keeping watch, and let the breath go calm and even underneath: the warrior in the spine, the sage in the breath. Many Vishnu devotees repeat a short name on each breath: Om Namo Narayanaya.
Say it silently for a few rounds. If you don't pray, just keep the two together, alert and quiet. Near the end, ask: what is my own dharma?

wordCard.voice: Parashurama: Rama with the axe, Vishnu's form as a sage's son born with a warrior's fire.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Rama with the axe; parashu means axe.

carryVoice: Your line: svadharma, your dharma follows your nature. Two bowls swapped, and sages raised a fighter. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 9.15 (Richika, Satyavati and the two portions; Jamadagni; the birth of Parashurama)
Vishnu Purana 4.7 (the swapped portions; Vishvamitra born to Gadhi's wife, Jamadagni to Satyavati)
Bhagavad Gita 4.13 (the four orders by guna and karma); 3.35 and 18.47 (better one's own dharma, imperfectly, than another's well)
